### Project Name

Agent Skills

### Project Description

Agent Skills are a lightweight, open format for extending AI agent capabilities with specialized knowledge and workflows. At its core, a skill is a folder containing a SKILL.md file; that file includes metadata (name and description, at minimum) and instructions that tell an agent how to perform a specific task. Skills can also bundle scripts, reference materials, templates, and other resources.

Agents are increasingly capable, but often don’t have the context they need to do real work reliably. Skills solve this by packaging procedural knowledge and company-, team-, and user-specific context into portable, version-controlled folders that agents load on demand. This gives agents domain expertise (specialized knowledge captured as reusable instructions and resources), repeatable workflows (multi-step tasks turned into consistent, auditable procedures), and cross-product reuse (build a skill once and use it across any skills-compatible agent).

Agents load skills through progressive disclosure, in three stages. Discovery: at startup, agents load only the name and description of each available skill. Activation: when a task matches a skill’s description, the agent reads the full SKILL.md instructions into context. Execution: the agent follows the instructions, optionally executing bundled code or loading referenced files as needed. Full instructions load only when a task calls for them, so agents can keep many skills on hand with only a small context footprint.

Anthropic developed the format, introduced it as a product capability on October 16, 2025, and published it as an open standard on December 18, 2025\. The specification, documentation, and a reference validation library are published at https://agentskills.io and https://github.com/agentskills/agentskills. As of September 21, 2026, the public Client Showcase (https://agentskills.io/clients) lists 46 agent products that have shipped support for the format, most of them built by organizations other than Anthropic.


### Alignment with AAIF Mission

The Foundation’s charter states that its mission is “to drive adoption and growth of open source agentic AI in the broader community.” Agent Skills advances that mission at a layer the Foundation’s portfolio does not yet cover, the packaging of agent capabilities.

**The format standardizes the capability layer the way MCP standardized the tool layer.** Every agent product needs an answer to how users and organizations package reusable knowledge and workflows for an agent, and before Skills each product answered it alone. A skill authored against the specification runs in any conforming client, collapsing per-product integration work exactly as MCP did for tool connectivity.

**Adoption already treats the format as shared infrastructure.** Implementers include agents and IDEs from Microsoft, Google, OpenAI, JetBrains, and AWS, among more than thirty others (see Evidence of Adoption below). The format’s governance has not caught up to its adoption, and this proposal is how it catches up.

**Contribution completes the move to neutral ownership.** The standard is already open, permissively licensed, developed in public, and open to contributions from the broader ecosystem. What Anthropic still holds is the canonical repository, the agentskills.io domain, the GitHub organization, and the name. Contributing those places them with a neutral owner.


### Relation to Existing AAIF Projects

**Model Context Protocol (MCP).** The two standards sit at adjacent layers and are used together. MCP is a runtime protocol that gives an agent access to tools, data, and applications; Agent Skills is a file format that gives an agent procedural knowledge, meaning what to do, in what order, with which tools. A SKILL.md can instruct an agent on when and how to use particular MCP tools, and the MCP community itself maintains a “Skills Over MCP” working-group charter.

**AGENTS.md.** The formats are complementary, and a project can use both. AGENTS.md, one of the Foundation’s inaugural projects, is an always-loaded instruction file scoped to a repository; it tells any agent how to work in that codebase. A skill is a self-contained, on-demand capability package, discoverable by its metadata, portable across repositories and agents, and able to bundle scripts and assets. In practice an AGENTS.md describes the project the agent is standing in, and skills describe capabilities the agent brings to any project. The ecosystems already overlap. OpenAI ships Agent Skills support in Codex, and clients such as Ona document the two formats side by side.

**Goose.** Goose implements Agent Skills and is listed on the Client Showcase.

**Agent2Agent Protocol (A2A).** A2A standardizes communication between independent agent systems; Agent Skills packages what a single agent knows how to do. 

**agentgateway and Agent Router.** agentgateway and Agent Router (formerly Envoy AI Gateway) address the infrastructure and traffic layer; Agent Skills addresses the capability layer. 

### Example Use Cases and Evidence of Adoption

Real-world usage takes two forms: organizations shipping skills, and products executing them.

**Organizations shipping skills.** 

* **Anthropic**. Agent Skills power Claude’s ability to create and edit documents in production; the skills behind them are public at https://github.com/anthropics/skills. 

* **AWS**. The Agent Toolkit for AWS ships agent skills, which AWS describes as “curated packages of instructions, code scripts, and reference materials that help AI coding agents complete specific AWS tasks” (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/agent-toolkit/latest/userguide/skills.html). 

* **Google**. The Google AI Edge Gallery ships skills in its repository.

* **Microsoft**. Microsoft publishes a catalog of skills for AI coding agents working with Azure SDKs and Microsoft AI Foundry.

**Products executing skills.** The public Client Showcase lists 46 agent products that have shipped Agent Skills support, most entries linking to that organization’s own published implementation documentation. Listing requires that the product be publicly available and able to discover and execute skills today; announced intent does not qualify. ### Governance Model

Anthropic leads the project today, and this contribution exists to bring other implementers into its governance. Anthropic has invited engineers from some organizations that ship production implementations of the format to join Anthropic’s maintainers as the initial members of the project’s Technical Steering Committee. The committee’s composition and decision rules will be settled with the Linux Foundation during onboarding, and the committee will be open to additional members over time. Current practice is described under Public-Facing Contribution Process and Leadership Team & Decision Process.

### CI/CD & Release Workflow

The project today is a specification, a documentation site, and a small Python reference library, and its release workflow reflects that.

* The specification and documentation are maintained as living documents on main and published continuously to https://agentskills.io (site built with Mintlify).  
* The skills-ref reference library (Python 3.11+) provides a validate command that checks a skill against the specification, with pytest and ruff declared as development dependencies.

AAIF onboarding will add GitHub Actions CI on every pull request (lint and tests for skills-ref, documentation build verification, link checking) and tagged and changelogged specification releases so implementers can target a specific version.

### Public-Facing Contribution Process for Specifications

The process is documented in CONTRIBUTING.md. Spec proposals, design questions, and feature requests go to GitHub Discussions; concrete bugs go to Issues; documentation improvements are welcomed by pull request. The policy asks that proposals “address real implementation challenges you’ve encountered, not theoretical concerns,” and states the bar applied to the spec itself: “We maintain a high bar for additions to the spec — it is much easier to add things to a specification than to remove them. Every new feature adds complexity that all implementers must understand and support.”

Under the project’s Technical Charter, to be adopted during onboarding, the project will add a formal, numbered proposal track for normative spec changes, comparable to MCP’s Specification Enhancement Proposal process, and a documented approval rule for spec changes. Today, spec changes are merged on GitHub without a written approval rule.

### Publicly Accessible Issue Tracker

https://github.com/agentskills/agentskills/issues (bugs) and https://github.com/agentskills/agentskills/discussions (proposals and design questions).

### External Project Dependencies

The specification itself is a documented file format with no software dependencies. The repository contains two software components.

skills-ref reference library (Python 3.11+):

| Dependency | Role | License |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| click \>= 8.0 | runtime | BSD-3-Clause |
| strictyaml \>= 1.7.3 | runtime | MIT |
| hatchling | build backend | MIT |
| pytest | development only | MIT |
| ruff | development only | MIT |

Documentation site: built and hosted with Mintlify, a proprietary hosted documentation platform. Mintlify is tooling for the docs site, not a dependency of the standard or of any implementation, and can be replaced with the Linux Foundation’s standard documentation infrastructure during onboarding if preferred.

### Maintainers & Contributors

**Maintainers.** The format was created at Anthropic, and the Anthropic employees listed below lead the project.

| Name | GitHub | Affiliation | Area |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Mahesh Murag | maheshmurag | Anthropic | Project lead, specification |
| David Soria Parra | dsp-ant | Anthropic | Specification |

**Contributors.** As of September 21, 2026, the repository has 145 commits on main from dozens of contributors; the full contributor list is at https://github.com/agentskills/agentskills/graphs/contributors.

Today the maintainers listed above are all at Anthropic. That changes with this contribution. The initial Technical Steering Committee described under Governance Model is expected to include engineers from other organizations alongside Anthropic’s maintainers, and MAINTAINERS.md will be published with that composition during onboarding. The breadth of independent implementation is why the step is overdue. Forty-four of the 46 products on the Client Showcase are built by organizations other than Anthropic, and Microsoft, Google, OpenAI, JetBrains, and AWS each maintain production implementations of a specification in which none of them has a formal voice.

### Leadership Team & Decision Process

The project is led by the Anthropic employees listed in the maintainer table above.

Today, decisions rest with the leadership team. There is no separate steering body. After acceptance, the project will operate under the Technical Charter and a published GOVERNANCE.md that defines maintainer roles and the spec-change approval rule.

### Roadmap

The next twelve months focus on hardening the specification and its governance.

* **Versioned specification releases.** Move from a living document to tagged releases with a changelog, so implementers can declare and test against a specific version.  
* **Formal spec-change process.** Publish a numbered proposal track for normative changes with a documented approval rule, replacing Discussions-based intake.  
* **Technical Steering Committee**. Constitute the committee with its initial multi-organization membership and publish the project’s governance documents.  
* **Security guidance.** Publish SECURITY.md and formal authoring and consumption guidance; stabilize or remove the experimental allowed-tools field.  
* **Project hygiene.** Add CI, pursue an OpenSSF Best Practices badge, and complete Linux Foundation onboarding (asset transfer, contribution policy, code of conduct).

### Security

The project will pursue an OpenSSF Best Practices badge as part of AAIF onboarding (a roadmap item above). The attack surface is small: a specification, a documentation site, and a Python validation library with two permissively licensed runtime dependencies. Onboarding will also add a published security policy with a vulnerability-disclosure process, and dependency and code scanning in CI.

Two commitments belong in this field because the format itself raises them. Skills can bundle executable scripts, and Anthropic’s launch guidance already warns that malicious skills can introduce vulnerabilities and directs users to install skills only from trusted sources and audit bundled code and dependencies (https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/equipping-agents-for-the-real-world-with-agent-skills); the project will formalize that guidance as published project documentation for skill authors and consumers. And the specification’s experimental allowed-tools field, a space-separated string of tools a skill is pre-approved to use, is security-relevant; it will be stabilized with clear semantics or removed before a versioned release.

### Details of Existing Financial Sponsorship

Anthropic funds and operates all project infrastructure: the GitHub organization, the agentskills.io domain, documentation hosting, and the community Discord. The project has no other sponsors and takes no membership fees or donations.

### Infrastructure Needs or Requests

Current infrastructure: GitHub (the agentskills organization), Mintlify for the documentation site, Discord for community chat; all would transfer to the Foundation. 

Requests: standard Linux Foundation project services and continuity for agentskills.io and the Discord through the transfer. No compute or cloud-credit needs at present.
